blocks.t: F i g u r e 14.1 Chemical equilibrium in the cobalt chloride–HCl system. (a) The pink color is due to the hexaaqua complex ion [Co(H2O)6]21. (b) The blue color is due to the tetrachloro complex ion [CoCl4]22. (c) Adding HCl to the pink solution in (a) converts some of the Co(II) to the tetrachloro complex. The lavender color is produced by the combination of pink hexaaqua species and blue tetrachloro species. (d) Adding water to the blue solution in (b) converts some of the Co(II) to the hexaaqua species. The combination of the two gives the lavender color. The same equilibrium state is reached by running the reaction from the left (c) and from the right (d).

Let’s start by observing a particular reaction that illustrates all the aspects of equilibrium we need to understand. We have selected the reactions of cobalt(II) ions in aqueous solutions in which chloride ion is also pre­sent because the progress and outcome of the reactions are directly visible. The cobalt(II) ions can form vari- ous different complex ions, depending on the amount of chloride pre­sent. For ex- ample, if CoCl2?6H2O is dissolved in pure water to the concentration 0.08 m, the resulting solution is pale pink in color due to the hexaaquacobalt(II) complex ion [Co(H2O)6]21 (Fig. 14.1a). If CoCl2?6H2O is dissolved in 10 m HCl to the concen- tration 0.08 m, the solution is deep blue due to the tetrachlorocobalt(II) complex ion [CoCl4]22 (see Fig. 14.1b). Solutions containing a mixture of both Co(II) spe- cies are lavender, as shown in Figure 14.1c, d.
The hexaaqua complex can be converted into the tetrachloro complex by reac- tion with chloride ion:
